match.reason: None of the bank points teaches how the sign of f′ relates to whether f rises or falls; the stationary points card only covers solving f′(x) = 0 and classifying turning points, which is related but a different idea.

draft.title: Graphs of derivative functions
card: The derivative f′(x) gives the gradient of the graph of f at each x. So its graph shows how steep f is and which way it slopes.
Where f rises as x increases, the gradient is positive, so f′ is above the x-axis. Where f falls, f′ is below the x-axis.
At a stationary point, the tangent is flat. The gradient is zero, so the graph of f′ touches or crosses the x-axis there.
Example: a curve falls until x = 2, then rises. So f′ is negative for x < 2, zero at x = 2 and positive for x > 2.
draft.remember: Read f′ from the slope of f: above the axis means rising, below means falling.

a.q: The graph of f falls for x < 1 and rises for x > 1. Which describes f′?
opts: Negative for x < 1, zero at x = 1, positive after
Positive for x < 1, zero at x = 1, negative after
Negative everywhere, with a zero at x = 1
Zero for x < 1 and positive for x > 1
a.why: A falling graph has a negative gradient, and a rising graph has a positive one. The flat point at x = 1 gives zero. Swapping the signs is the tempting mistake.

b.q: The graph of f has a peak at x = −1 and a dip at x = 3. Where is f′ negative?
opts: Between x = −1 and x = 3
For x < −1 and for x > 3
Only at x = −1 and x = 3
Between x = −1 and x = 3, and nowhere else is zero
b.why: After a peak the graph falls until the dip, so f′ is negative between −1 and 3. Outside that interval f rises, so f′ is positive. The values −1 and 3 are where f′ is zero, not negative.
b.clue: What does the graph do just after a peak?

a.best: Negative for x < 1, zero at x = 1, positive after

also_right: Between x = −1 and x = 3, and nowhere else is zero

problems.detail: The option 'Between x = −1 and x = 3, and nowhere else is zero' is ungrammatical and unclear. Read as 'and nowhere else', it is also right, so the question has two defensible answers. Reword or replace this distractor.

The question assumes the peak and dip are the only stationary points, but never says so. Without that, f′ need not be negative on the whole interval or positive outside it. Add 'and has no other stationary points'.

check.summary: Question b has a garbled distractor ('…and nowhere else is zero') that can be read as a second right answer. It also never states that the peak and dip are the only stationary points. The card and question a are fine.

final.title: Graphs of derivative functions
card: The derivative f′(x) gives the gradient of the graph of \(f\) at each \(x\). So its graph shows how steep \(f\) is and which way it slopes.
Where \(f\) rises as \(x\) increases, the gradient is positive, so f′ is above the x-axis. Where \(f\) falls, f′ is below the x-axis.
At a stationary point, such as a peak or a dip, the tangent is flat. The gradient is zero, so the graph of f′ touches or crosses the x-axis there.
Example: a curve falls until \(x = 2\), then rises. So f′ is negative for \(x < 2\), zero at \(x = 2\) and positive for \(x > 2\).

4.alt: The curve \(y = f(x) = (x - 2)^{2} - 1\) falls until \(x = 2\), then rises. Its derivative \(y = f'(x) = 2x - 4\) is below the x-axis for \(x < 2\), crosses it at \(x = 2\), where \(f\) is flat, and is above it for \(x > 2\).

final.remember: Read f′ from the slope of \(f\): above the axis means rising, below means falling.
